content: The number of men who would miss treatment due to false positives from the test, or who would be falsely treated due to false negatives, was calculated. Subsequently, the costs associated with the flowcharts, point-of-care tests, and the potential costs of antimicrobial resistance development were determined. A mathematical model was developed and executed using Excel. The following assumptions were made based on current literature and hypotheses: 1. The prevalence of Neisseria gonorrhoeae (NG) and Chlamydia trachomatis (CT) in men with urethral discharge was assumed to be 10%, 40%, or 60%, while the prevalence of NG alone was assumed to be 5%, 20%, or 30%, based on included studies. 2. Among men with both CT and NG, the distribution of true cases was assumed to be 75% CT and 25% NG, based on included studies. 3. The cure rates for CT and NG with treatment were assumed to be 94% and 98%, respectively, while adverse event rates were 15% for CT and 3% for NG. 4. The sensitivity and specificity of point-of-care tests were modeled at various levels: 60% and 90%, 70% and 80%, 70% and 90%, 80% and 80%, and 80% and 90%. 5. Costs for flowcharts and point-of-care tests were calculated, but costs related to repeat testing, treatment, or future antimicrobial resistance were not included. Six eligible studies, involving a total of 1,570 participants, were included in the analysis. All studies evaluated flowcharts against reference tests for NG and/or CT. Most studies were conducted in Asia, and none specified whether participants had persistent or non-persistent urethral discharge. The pooled diagnostic accuracy of syndromic management for NG and/or CT infections was reported, but the certainty of evidence was low due to the limited number of events across studies. Specificity was calculable in only one of the pooled studies. Flowchart 1 relied on history and risk assessment, Flowchart 2 included genital examination, and Flowchart 3 incorporated history, risk assessment, genital examination, and Gram staining/microscopy of urethral discharge samples. No studies assessed other country-specific flowcharts. Modeling results showed that 30 to 90 men per 1,000 missed treatment with syndromic management using Flowcharts 1, 2, or 3. In high-prevalence settings (60% NG/CT), the number of men who missed treatment ranged from 120 to 240 per 1,000 with point-of-care tests, but this number was reduced to 30 with GeneXpert. In low-prevalence settings (10% NG/CT), the number ranged from 20 to 40 per 1,000, and was reduced to 5 with GeneXpert. The number of men falsely treated ranged from 40 to 80 per 1,000 with point-of-care tests in high-prevalence settings, and 8 with GeneXpert. In low-prevalence settings, the number ranged from 90 to 180 per 1,000, and 18 with GeneXpert. The costs of using flowcharts were lower than point-of-care tests, regardless of NG/CT prevalence. GeneXpert had the highest cost (~$20,000), while Flowchart 2 was the cheapest (~$4,500). The study highlighted the need for further research to evaluate the diagnostic accuracy of syndromic management strategies and to increase the certainty of pooled estimates. Future modeling could explore the use of these tests in broader populations, such as men presenting with other risk factors for NG/CT, to determine cost-effectiveness and improve treatment accuracy.
